segments.t: A jump server (bastion host) acts as an intermediate gateway to reach servers on a private network. korTTY tunnels the connection through a jump server so you can reach an internal system from your local machine without direct network access to it.

korTTY authenticates to the jump server with the jump server's own credentials, opens a tunnel through it, and then opens the real SSH session to the target host through that tunnel. The target's credentials are used only for the target, and the jump server's credentials only for the jump server — neither host is offered the other's password or key.

Both SSH terminal and SFTP connections to the target route through the jump server; there is nothing extra to configure for SFTP. This works whatever the target's own authentication is — password, keyboard-interactive, SSH key or a temporary SSH key: a stored jump server password is decrypted with your master password in every case.

Mosh connections cannot go through a jump server: a Mosh session runs over UDP, which the jump server's SSH tunnel (TCP) does not forward. korTTY refuses the combination up front — the Jump Server tab warns as soon as it is configured, and connecting fails immediately with a clear message instead of stalling after the SSH bootstrap. Use the SSH protocol for targets behind a bastion, or disable the jump server.
To configure a jump server for a connection:
Open the KTPH000Connection ManagerKTPH001 and edit (or create) a connection.
Go to the KTPH000Jump ServerKTPH001 tab.
KTPH000Jump server hostKTPH001 — hostname or IP address of the jump server
KTPH000UsernameKTPH001 — login username for the jump server
KTPH000PasswordKTPH001 — the password is stored encrypted with your master password. Leave the field empty when editing to keep the previously stored password.
KTPH000SSH key file (no passphrase)KTPH001 — the path to an unencrypted private key file. Passphrase-protected keys are not supported for the jump hop.
When the jump server cannot be usedKTPH000

korTTY decrypts a stored jump server password before it contacts the jump server. If the stored jump password cannot be used — none is stored, the master password vault is locked, or the stored value cannot be decrypted — connecting stops at once with a message that says so, without contacting the jump server, without asking about its host key and without working through the retry count. Unlock the vault with KTPH000Configuration KTPH006 Security KTPH007 Unlock Vault…KTPH001 (see KTPH002Unlocking the vault laterKTPH003) or store the password in the connection's KTPH004Jump ServerKTPH005 tab, then reconnect.

An incomplete jump setup (no username, or key authentication without a usable key file) and a jump-server host key you rejected are also reported once instead of being retried, because another attempt would fail identically. A jump server that cannot be reached, or a network error on the way, is still retried like any other connection failure.

The jump server's host key is verified on first use exactly like any other host: korTTY shows the key's SHA-256 fingerprint and asks you to confirm it, then pins it. On later connections a changed jump-server key is refused, the same trust-on-first-use protection the target host gets. When the connection was opened from a terminal tab or the SFTP manager, the changed-key alert offers KTPH000Review and Replace…KTPH001 for the jump server as well, under the same rules as for the target (see KTPH002SSH host-key verificationKTPH003). The bastion is always checked strictly: KTPH004relaxing host-key verificationKTPH005 applies to target hosts only, never to the jump hop.

This holds even when host-key verification has been relaxed for the target: the per-connection, per-group and global opt-outs never cover the bastion, so its key is always verified strictly. See KTPH000Relaxing host-key verificationKTPH001.
The target host is verified under its own name even though the transport goes through the tunnel, so a compromised bastion cannot substitute a different target host key unnoticed.
Target servers are behind a firewall and only reachable through a bastion host.
Security policy requires routing through a gateway.
Internal infrastructure uses private addresses and needs an intermediary for access.

Jump server passwords are stored encrypted with your master password, alongside the connection's own credentials. Because the stored password is never shown back, editing the connection with an empty jump-server password field keeps the stored one; type a new value only to change it. If the master password vault is locked when you save a new jump password, korTTY offers KTPH000Unlock Vault…KTPH001; if the vault stays locked, korTTY says that the jump server password cannot be saved, keeps the stored password as it was, and still saves the other settings of the connection.
